question.problem:
Three doors in a computer game hide an apple, and another door hides an orange. Fifteen players are playing the game, and each player is asked to choose one of the four doors at random. 
What is the probability that at least $14$ players will win an apple? Round your answer to $4$ decimal places.
question.worked_solution:
Let the random variable $X$ be the number of players winning an apple.

Here, we have the following information:

- there are $n=15$ players in the game

- the probability of choosing a door that hides an apple is $p=\frac{3}{4}$

So, $X$ follows a binomial distribution, where $X∼B(15,\frac{3}{4}).$ 

The number of successes of a binomial random variable has the probability mass function

$$
P(X=x)=(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{n}{x}){p}^{x}(1-p)^{n-x},
$$

where $n$ is the number of experiments, and $p$ is the probability of success on each experiment.

Substituting the above information into the formula for probability mass function, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X=x) & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{15}{x}){(\frac{3}{4})}^{x}{(1-\frac{3}{4})}^{15-x} \\  & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{15}{x}){(\frac{3}{4})}^{x}{(\frac{1}{4})}^{15-x}.\end{aligned}
$$

We want to find the probability that at least $14$ players will win an apple. So, we compute

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\ge 14) & =P(X=14)+P(X=15) \\  & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{15}{14}){(\frac{3}{4})}^{14}{(\frac{1}{4})}^{15-14}+(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{15}{15}){(\frac{3}{4})}^{15}{(\frac{1}{4})}^{15-15} \\  & =15{(\frac{3}{4})}^{14}{(\frac{1}{4})}^{1}+1{(\frac{3}{4})}^{15}{(\frac{1}{4})}^{0} \\  & ≈0.0802\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $4$ decimal places.
